01.r: The crowd is still listening when Jesus goes on.
01.n: A present participle in the genitive with its subject, a construction that sets the scene: literally 'they hearing these things'. The present tense means the listening is still going on.

03.r: The listeners; the verse does not name them.
03.n: The BSB's 'the people' names the listeners; the Greek has only 'they'.

04.r: What Jesus has just been saying.

05.r: Jesus goes on to say more.
05.n: An aorist participle, literally 'having added, he spoke'. Abbott-Smith gives 'to add, join to, give in addition' and notes that the Septuagint uses the verb chiefly for Hebrew יָסַף; the phrasing likely echoes that Hebrew idiom for doing something again or further (an inference).

06.r: He tells the parable that follows.
06.n: The verb is the usual 'said'; English cannot 'say' a parable, so this study writes 'spoke' here.

07.r: A story told to set one thing beside another.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives the root senses 'a placing beside, juxtaposition' and 'a comparing, comparison', and notes that the Septuagint uses it for Hebrew מָשָׁל. The YLT's 'simile' keeps the idea of comparison.

08.r: Gives the two reasons for the parable.
08.n: A preposition with the article and an infinitive: literally 'because of the being near'. It covers both reasons that follow.

09.r: The article that turns the infinitives into a noun phrase after 'because'.

10.r: Jesus is close to the city.
10.n: Abbott-Smith classes it here as a preposition with the genitive, 'near', and cites this verse.

11.n: A present infinitive, literally 'being'. English needs a finite verb.

13.n: The subject of the infinitive, in the accusative. Listed as not in the Textus Receptus; English needs a subject in either case.

15.r: The listeners' belief about what was about to happen.
15.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to be of opinion, suppose'. It reports what they supposed, not what the text endorses.

18.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'on the spot, forthwith, instantly', and notes that it stands for παρὰ τὸ χρῆμα, roughly 'at the thing itself' (our gloss). The Geneva's 'shortly' softens it.

19.r: Something on the verge of happening.
19.n: A present tense in the Greek, 'is about', kept from their own expectation; English reported speech shifts it to 'was about'. Abbott-Smith gives 'to be about to be or do'.

21.r: God's royal rule, expected to show itself openly.
21.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is abstract: 'sovereignty, royal power, dominion'. The YLT's 'reign' brings out that sense.

22.r: Greek puts the article before God; English does not.

24.n: A present passive infinitive. Abbott-Smith gives the passive as 'to appear, be made manifest' and cites this verse.

tr_note: Our sources list αὐτόν, 'he', as absent from the Textus Receptus here. English needs a subject either way, so the KJV's 'because he was nigh' shows no difference.
